meteorShower.title: How meteor showers form
meteorShower.summary: A comet keeps shedding dust along its orbit, gradually building a dust trail. When the Earth crosses that trail, the dust burns up in the atmosphere as a meteor shower.
meteorShower.credit: Orbits and geometry computed with astronomy-engine; body sizes are exaggerated so the geometry stays legible

moon.title: Tour the Moon: craters, maria and landing sites
moon.summary: Roam the near and far side with NASA's LROC colour imagery and LOLA elevation data. Rotate, zoom, and use adjustable raking light to read the Moon's real terrain.
moon.hint: Drag to orbit · wheel/pinch to zoom · arrow keys refine a site view · click a feature to descend

oceanus-procellarum.title: Oceanus Procellarum
oceanus-procellarum.body: The largest of the lunar maria, covering about four million square kilometres. It is not one crater but an ancient lowland flooded by basalt lava, which is why it counts as an ocean rather than a sea.

mare-imbrium.title: Mare Imbrium
mare-imbrium.body: An impact about 3.8 billion years ago excavated a basin some 1,145 km across, and lava later filled it. The ridges still visible around the edge are ejecta thrown out by that impact.

mare-ser-enitatis.title: Mare Serenitatis
mare-ser-enitatis.body: The dark basalt of the Sea of Serenity is roughly a billion years younger than the surrounding highlands. Apollo 17 landed on its eastern edge, in the Taurus–Littrow valley.

mare-tranquillitatis.title: Mare Tranquillitatis
mare-tranquillitatis.body: A basalt plain about 873 km wide, darker than the highlands because its iron- and titanium-rich lava reflects less light. It is also where humans first walked on the Moon.

mare-crisium.title: Mare Crisium
mare-crisium.body: An isolated circular mare about 555 km across, ringed by mountains. Sitting near the eastern limb, it librates in and out of view from Earth.

mare-orientale.title: Mare Orientale
mare-orientale.body: One of the youngest large multi-ring impact basins on the Moon, on the south-western limb where it is hard to see whole from Earth. Its concentric rings are a textbook impact-basin structure.

south-pole-aitken.title: South Pole–Aitken basin
south-pole-aitken.body: One of the largest impact structures in the Solar System: about 2,500 km across and 13 km deep, mostly on the far side. Chang'e 4 landed inside it, in Von Kármán crater.

tycho.title: Tycho
tycho.body: Eighty-five kilometres across and relatively young at about 100 million years, Tycho has the Moon's most conspicuous ray system — binoculars will show it on any full moon.

copernicus.title: Copernicus
copernicus.body: A 93 km complex crater with a central peak and terraced walls, formed about 800 million years ago. Its rays are fainter than Tycho's, which makes it a useful marker for dating lunar terrain.

aristarchus.title: Aristarchus
aristarchus.body: One of the brightest features on the near side, roughly twice as reflective as the surrounding mare. It sits on the Aristarchus plateau, next to the winding volcanic rille called Schröter's Valley.

clavius.title: Clavius
clavius.body: At 231 km across, Clavius is among the largest craters on the near side. It is very old: later impacts have flattened and pockmarked its floor, and a chain of younger craters overlaps its southern rim.

tsiolkovskiy.title: Tsiolkovskiy
tsiolkovskiy.body: A far-side crater whose floor is flooded with dark basalt, making it one of the most recognisable landmarks on the lunar far side. The far-side crust is thicker, so such dark floors are rare.

shackleton.title: Shackleton
shackleton.body: Near the south pole, where crater floors never see sunlight and rank among the coldest places in the Solar System, possibly preserving water ice. It is a focus for lunar south-pole exploration.

apollo-11.title: Apollo 11 landing site
apollo-11.body: In July 1969 Eagle touched down at Tranquility Base, and Armstrong and Aldrin spent about 21 hours on the surface. The descent stage, instruments and footprints are still there.

apollo-12.title: Apollo 12 landing site
apollo-12.body: In November 1969 Intrepid landed within walking distance of Surveyor 3, which had been sitting on the Ocean of Storms since 1967. The crew brought parts of it home, so it is the only spacecraft ever visited on another world.

apollo-14.title: Apollo 14 landing site
apollo-14.body: In February 1971 Shepard and Mitchell came down in the Fra Mauro highlands, the terrain Apollo 13 had been aiming for. They climbed Cone crater on foot, hauling a hand cart of samples up the slope.

apollo-15.title: Apollo 15 landing site
apollo-15.body: In July 1971 Scott and Irwin landed at Hadley–Apennine, between the Apennine mountains and Hadley Rille, and drove the first Lunar Roving Vehicle. They returned the Genesis Rock, an anorthosite dating to the Moon's original crust.

apollo-16.title: Apollo 16 landing site
apollo-16.body: In April 1972 Young and Duke set down in the Descartes highlands, expecting to find volcanic terrain and finding impact breccia instead — a result that rewrote part of the lunar geologic map.

apollo-17.title: Apollo 17 landing site
apollo-17.body: The last crewed landing, in December 1972, came down in the Taurus–Littrow valley. Geologist Harrison Schmitt found the famous orange soil there, erupted about 3.6 billion years ago.

change-3.title: Chang'e 3 landing site
change-3.body: In December 2013 Chang'e 3 made a soft landing in southern Sinus Iridum, and Yutu became the first rover to drive on the Moon since 1976.

change-4.title: Chang'e 4 landing site
change-4.body: In January 2019 Chang'e 4 landed in Von Kármán crater, inside the South Pole–Aitken basin — the first soft landing on the far side. Yutu-2 is still roving.

change-5.title: Chang'e 5 landing site
change-5.body: In December 2020 Chang'e 5 sampled and returned 1,731 grams of lunar material from near Mons Rümker — the first sample return in 44 years.

luna-21.title: Luna 21 and Lunokhod 2
luna-21.body: Luna 21 landed inside Le Monnier crater on the eastern rim of Mare Serenitatis in January 1973 and deployed Lunokhod 2, which went on to drive about 39 kilometres — further than any other rover, and its wheel tracks are still visible from orbit.

apollo-11-tranquility-base.title: Tranquility Base, looking south-west
apollo-11-tranquility-base.caption: Apollo 11, 20 July 1969. Photographed from about ten metres west of the Lunar Module Eagle's plus-Z footpad, looking toward the south-west at the crater rim Armstrong had spotted from the window during the descent.

apollo-11-armstrong-crater.title: Armstrong's crater from Tranquility Base
apollo-11-armstrong-crater.caption: Apollo 11, 20 July 1969. A crater Armstrong called out during the descent, with the Lunar Module and flag at the left edge and the photographer's own shadow at the right.

apollo-12-surveyor-crater.title: Surveyor Crater from the rim
apollo-12-surveyor-crater.caption: Apollo 12, November 1969. Taken from north-east of Intrepid, sweeping west past the flag and then round into Surveyor Crater, where Surveyor 3 had landed two and a half years earlier.

apollo-14-fra-mauro.title: Toward the western horizon
apollo-14-fra-mauro.caption: Apollo 14, February 1971. A sweep across the Fra Mauro formation toward the western horizon, from the terrain Shepard and Mitchell crossed on foot.

apollo-15-hadley-rille.title: Hadley Rille and the Lunar Roving Vehicle
apollo-15-hadley-rille.caption: Apollo 15, August 1971. David Scott at the Lunar Roving Vehicle on the edge of Hadley Rille, photographed by James Irwin south of Station 2.

apollo-16-station-1.title: Station 1, Descartes highlands
apollo-16-station-1.caption: Apollo 16, April 1972. Charles Duke collecting samples at Station 1 while John Young photographs him, on the first moonwalk of the mission.

apollo-17-station-2.title: Station 2, Taurus–Littrow
apollo-17-station-2.caption: Apollo 17, December 1972. The second moonwalk: the parked Lunar Roving Vehicle and astronaut footprints across the valley floor, with the South Massif ridge beyond.

apollo-17-station-5.title: Station 5, on the edge of Camelot
apollo-17-station-5.caption: Apollo 17, December 1972. Boulders and the shoulder of the North Massif at Station 5, looking toward the massif. The strip covers most of the horizon but its two ends do not meet, so turning stops at the edge of the photograph.

change-4-farside-lander.title: The far side of the Moon, from Chang'e 4
change-4-farside-lander.caption: Chang'e 4, January 2019. The first panorama taken from the lunar far side: the lander's solar panels and the Yutu-2 rover's tracks inside Von Kármán crater, in the South Pole–Aitken basin.

eclipses.title: Solar and lunar eclipses
eclipses.summary: Solar and lunar eclipses both come from a near-alignment of the Sun, Earth and Moon: the Moon's shadow sweeps Earth during a solar eclipse, while the Moon crosses Earth's shadow during a lunar eclipse. Switch sections to compare the umbra, penumbra and antumbra, and see why eclipses do not happen every month.
eclipses.hint: Drag to rotate · scroll to zoom · switch section and view in the control panel · space to play or pause · R to reset
eclipses.credit: Eclipse times, peak locations and body positions computed with astronomy-engine; the system view is schematic and not to scale

guide.title: Solar and lunar eclipse guide
guide.solarAlignment: At new Moon, the Moon lies between the Sun and Earth. A solar eclipse occurs where its shadow crosses the ground. Sizes and distances in this system view are schematic.
guide.solarPartial: From this observing site, the Moon gradually covers the Sun. During a partial eclipse, direct viewing requires certified solar protection; ordinary sunglasses are unsafe.
guide.solarTotal: Only when the Moon completely hides the photosphere does the corona appear. Its look is based on a 2024 photograph, while the overlap follows this event. Restore eye protection as soon as sunlight reappears.
guide.lunarAlignment: At full Moon, Earth lies between the Sun and Moon. A lunar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes through Earth's shadow on the side away from the Sun.
guide.lunarPartial: The Moon first crosses the faint penumbra, then enters the umbra. Here the umbra progressively covers its face, with the boundary following the calculated angular geometry.
guide.lunarTotal: Once wholly inside the umbra, the Moon appears copper-red from sunlight refracted through Earth's atmosphere. This colour is an illustration, not a brightness forecast.
guide.inclination: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5.1° to the ecliptic. Only a new or full Moon near an orbital node can line the three bodies up closely enough for an eclipse.

labels.sunAbout: The Sun is about 1.392 million km across, roughly 109 Earth diameters. Its mean distance from Earth is about 149.6 million km, a light-travel time of about 8 minutes 20 seconds. Because the Sun is a finite disc rather than a point source, shadows divide into an umbra, penumbra and antumbra.
labels.earthAbout: Earth’s equatorial radius is about 6378 km. During a lunar eclipse it casts a shadow away from the Sun; at the Moon's distance the umbra's radius is about 4600 km, roughly 2.65 lunar radii. The Moon can therefore fit wholly inside it, and the total phase of a long lunar eclipse can exceed an hour.
labels.moonAbout: The Moon’s radius is 1737.4 km, about 0.27 of Earth’s, and its mean distance from Earth is about 384,400 km. Its orbital plane is tilted 5.145 degrees to the ecliptic, so at most new and full moons it passes above or below the Sun or Earth's shadow and no eclipse occurs.
labels.umbraAbout: The umbra is the region from which the light source is completely hidden. Earth’s umbra has a radius of about 4600 km at the Moon; when the whole Moon enters it, a total lunar eclipse occurs. The Moon’s umbra is usually narrow where it reaches Earth, so the path of a total solar eclipse is narrow too.
labels.penumbraAbout: The penumbra is the region where the source is only partly hidden. A penumbral lunar eclipse occurs when the Moon enters only Earth's penumbra and misses the umbra, usually producing subtle shading. The Moon's penumbra covers a much wider area of Earth than its umbra, so partial solar eclipses are visible over a larger region.
labels.antumbraAbout: When the Moon's apparent diameter is smaller than the Sun's, the umbra closes before reaching Earth and the region beyond its tip is the antumbra. From there the Moon sits wholly inside the solar disc, leaving a brilliant ring. The sky does not darken as it does in totality, and the full corona is not visible.
labels.ascendingNodeAbout: One of the two points where the Moon’s orbit crosses the ecliptic, here moving from south to north. A new or full moon must occur near a node for an eclipse to happen. The node line slowly regresses westward, completing a circuit in about 18.6 years.
labels.descendingNodeAbout: The other crossing, where the Moon moves from north of the ecliptic to south. The period when the Sun is near the node line is an eclipse season. Each lasts about 35 days and repeats just short of six months later, usually producing two and occasionally three solar or lunar eclipses.
labels.eclipticPlaneAbout: The plane of Earth’s orbit around the Sun; its projection on the sky is the ecliptic, the reference for ecliptic longitude and latitude. Eclipses require the Moon to be near this plane, which is why the ecliptic's name is tied to eclipses.
labels.lunarPlaneAbout: The plane of the Moon’s orbit around Earth, tilted 5.145 degrees from the ecliptic. That tilt explains why eclipses do not happen every month: only a new or full moon near a node can produce one. Set the tilt to zero and every new and full moon produces some kind of eclipse.
labels.peakAbout: For a solar eclipse, greatest eclipse is the instant when the Moon's shadow axis passes closest to Earth's centre. This marker is the surface point intersected by, or nearest to, that axis then. It is usually near the centre path but is not necessarily the point of longest totality or annularity. The observer starts here and can be moved off the central path.
labels.observerAbout: The place you have chosen to stand. The discs in the observer view are drawn from this point’s horizon coordinates and the real angular diameters, so nudging the position is enough to turn a total eclipse into a partial one.

panel.title: Eclipses
panel.teachingNote: Teaching assumption: the Moon's orbit is set flat against the ecliptic. Its real tilt is about 5.1 degrees, so an eclipse requires new or full moon to occur near a node.
panel.sunBelow: The Sun is below the horizon here, so this place sees nothing. The discs above still show the real alignment.
panel.solarTotalityNote: During totality the Moon completely hides the Sun's bright photosphere, revealing the normally faint corona. Its appearance is based on a real photograph; the Moon's position, size and phase still follow the selected event's geometry.
panel.lunarTotalityNote: A totally eclipsed Moon appears copper-red because sunlight refracted through Earth's atmosphere still reaches it; shorter wavelengths are preferentially scattered along the way. The colour and brightness here are approximate.
panel.solarSafetyNote: Eye safety: except during the brief total phase when the Sun's photosphere is completely covered, looking directly at the Sun requires certified solar-viewing protection. Ordinary sunglasses are unsafe.
panel.solarImageCredit: Corona appearance: NASA/Keegan Barber, 8 April 2024 total solar eclipse; not a photograph of the selected event.
panel.lunarImageCredit: Lunar surface: NASA SVS / LROC WAC near-side map; Earth's shadow and red tint are dynamic illustrations.
panel.lunarSkyNote: The lunar eclipse as seen from Earth's centre: the Moon crosses Earth's penumbral and umbral discs, with the Moon and both shadow discs drawn at their angular sizes for that instant.
panel.solarSkyAria: The Sun and Moon discs as seen from the observer, drawn at their real angular sizes and separation
panel.lunarSkyAria: The Moon's disc and the Earth's shadow discs as seen from the Earth's centre, drawn at their real angular sizes
panel.scaleNote: The system view is schematic: body sizes are exaggerated separately and the Sun-Earth distance is heavily compressed (the real distance is about 389 times the mean Earth-Moon distance). Directions and instants come from the ephemeris.
panel.legendAria: Which phase each band on the timeline marks
